    Chat templates & special tokens

    After this lesson you can explain why chat formatting is a correctness issue, use the tokenizer's own chat template, and recognize the silent failure that a template mismatch causes.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: Anatomy of an SFT example: prompt, completion, and the loss mask Verified: 12 Nov 2026

    An instruct model wasn't trained on bare text — it was trained on conversations formatted in a very specific way, with special tokens marking who is speaking. If you feed it a different format, you push it off the data it understands, and quality collapses. This is one of the most common silent failures in fine-tuning, and it's entirely avoidable.

    Roles and special tokens

    A chat is a list of messages, each with a role: system (standing instructions), user (the human), and assistant (the model). To turn that list into a single token stream, the model's training used special tokens — control tokens in the vocabulary that aren't ordinary text — to delimit each turn. Different model families use different markers; one common style looks like:

    <|im_start|>system

    You are a helpful assistant.<|im_end|>

    <|im_start|>user

    Classify: I loved it<|im_end|>

    <|im_start|>assistant

    positive<|im_end|>

    The chat template does this for you

    Every instruct tokenizer ships a chat template — a rule that turns a messages list into exactly the formatted string that model expects. tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False) returns that formatted string with the right special tokens; called with its defaults (transformers v5) it tokenizes too and returns a BatchEncoding (input_ids + attention_mask); add return_tensors="pt" and pass it as model.generate(**enc). Either way, the template, not you, decides the format. The cardinal rule:

    The double-BOS trap

    Many templates already put the beginning-of-sequence token in the string. If you render with tokenize=False and then call tokenizer(text), the tokenizer adds a second BOS (Mistral-7B-Instruct's tokenizer does exactly this). Pass add_special_tokens=False when you tokenize a rendered template, or let apply_chat_template tokenize for you.

    Key idea

    Use the model's own chat template for both training and inference, and never hand-format. The format you train on must match the format you serve on. When you fine-tune an instruct model, both must match the template it was aligned with; when you fine-tune a base model, you pick a template, and train/serve consistency is what matters.

    The generation prompt

    At inference you pass the system + user messages and set add_generation_prompt=True. That appends the opening of the assistant turn (e.g. <|im_start|>assistant) so the model knows it's now its turn to speak and starts generating the response. During training you don't add it — the assistant turn is already present as the completion.

    Where templates meet the loss mask

    Combine this with the previous lesson: the chat template lays out the full conversation, and the loss mask is set so that only the assistant content (plus its end token) is a learning target. Don't assume the tooling does this by default: TRL's SFTTrainer masks the prompt on prompt–completion data, but on messages data it trains on every token unless you set assistant_only_loss=True, which needs a template with {% generation %} markers (SmolLM2's has none). Decode the tokens whose label isn't -100 for one batch to check.

    The silent failure

    A template mismatch rarely errors. You'll see a plausible training loss and then garbage or oddly formatted outputs at inference. If a freshly fine-tuned model behaves strangely, check the chat template first — it's the usual culprit.

    Recap

    • An instruct model was trained on conversations laid out with special tokens, and its chat template produces exactly that layout; use it for both training and serving and never hand-format.
    • At inference set add_generation_prompt=True to open the assistant turn; in training the assistant turn is already the completion. When you tokenize a rendered template, pass add_special_tokens=False to avoid a double BOS.
    • A template mismatch rarely errors: you get a plausible loss and then odd outputs, so check the template first when a fine-tuned model misbehaves.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Run the script: it renders the same two messages with and without add_generation_prompt. What text does the generation prompt add, how many tokens is that, does tokenizing the rendered string again change the ids, and what happens if you pass only a user message?

    from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct")
msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Classify: I loved it"}]
a = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False)
b = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
print(repr(b[len(a):]))
print(len(tok(a, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids), len(tok(b, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids))
print(tok(b).input_ids == tok(b, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids)
user_only = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs[1:], tokenize=False)
print(repr(user_only[:90]))
    Show answer

    The generation prompt adds '<|im_start|>assistant\n', which is 4 tokens (22 become 26: <|im_start|>, ass, istant, newline). Tokenizing the rendered string again gives identical ids (True) because SmolLM2's tokenizer adds no BOS; the double-BOS trap needs a template and tokenizer that do. With a user-only message the template silently prepends a system prompt, You are a helpful AI assistant named SmolLM, trained by Hugging Face, so it ends up in your training text without you writing it.

    Key terms

    Chat template
    A tokenizer rule that converts a messages list into the exact formatted string the model expects.
    Role
    Who is speaking: system, user, or assistant.
    Special/control tokens
    Non-text tokens (e.g. turn delimiters) the model was trained with.
    apply_chat_template
    The function that renders messages with the model's template: a string with tokenize=False, a BatchEncoding (input_ids + attention_mask) by default.
    add_generation_prompt
    At inference, appends the assistant-turn opener so the model starts responding.
